questions.stem: A function $f: X \to Y$ between topological spaces is continuous if and only if:

options.text: The preimage of every open set in $Y$ is open in $X$.
options.explanation: This is the topological definition of continuity. It generalises the metric-space definition without requiring any notion of distance.

options.text: The image of every open set in $X$ is open in $Y$.
options.explanation: That is the definition of an open map, not a continuous map. Continuous maps need not be open.

options.text: $f$ is differentiable at every point of $X$.
options.explanation: Differentiability is a stronger condition requiring a metric and more structure. Topological continuity makes no reference to derivatives.

options.text: The preimage of every closed set in $Y$ is closed in $X$.
options.explanation: Actually this IS equivalent to continuity (since closed sets are complements of open sets, and preimages commute with complements). But the standard stated definition uses open sets.

options.text: An arbitrary product of compact topological spaces is compact.
options.explanation: Even an uncountable product of compact spaces (e.g., $[0,1]^{[0,1]}$) is compact. The proof for infinite products uses the Axiom of Choice.

options.text: A finite product of compact spaces is compact.
options.explanation: True but weaker. The remarkable content of Tychonoff's theorem is that it holds for arbitrary (including infinite) products.

options.text: A compact Hausdorff space is metrizable.
options.explanation: That is Urysohn's metrization theorem, a different result. Tychonoff's theorem is about products.

options.text: Every closed subset of a compact space is compact.
options.explanation: Also true, but a different result. Tychonoff's theorem is specifically about products.

questions.stem: The fundamental group $\pi_1(S^1)$ of the circle $S^1$ is isomorphic to:

options.explanation: A loop on the circle is characterised by its winding number: how many times it wraps around. The winding number is an integer, and concatenation of loops adds winding numbers. So $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
The trivial fundamental group would mean every loop can be contracted to a point. On the circle, a loop wrapping around once cannot be contracted.
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is the fundamental group of the projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$, not the circle.
The fundamental group of $S^1$ is the additive group of integers $\mathbb{Z}$ (discrete winding numbers), not the reals.
